capabilities.target: orders system order history and payment details

inputs.source: requests from support staff over SSO authenticated channel

instructions.note: The prompt says to process refund requests and use judgment on partial refunds, but gives no policy constraints for eligibility, amount limits beyond processor maximums, or dispute handling.
The instruction "Do not ask for confirmation" pushes the agent to act on irreversible refunds without a second check.

controls.name: Replace shared processor service account with per-user delegated or tightly scoped refund authority
Require human approval for refund issuance above low-risk thresholds or all refunds
Bind each refund to immutable request provenance including staff identity and rationale
Prompt instructs the agent to check the order before issuing the refund
controls.decay_rationale: This relies on the model following underspecified instructions and can be weakened by stronger rationalization or purpose drift around what counts as a justified refund.

findings.title: Irreversible refunds can be issued from trusted staff requests without approval or per-request provenance

attack_path.note: Authenticated support staff request enters the agent context.
The agent reads order history and payment details to decide the amount.
The agent issues an irreversible refund using shared processor authority.

evidence.observation: The prompt directs the agent to process refund requests, use its judgment on partial refunds, and not ask for confirmation, so refund issuance is autonomous for this path.
Refunds are irreversible once settled, usually within a day, making cap.issue_refund an S3 sink.
No approval gate is described for refunds; the agent acts directly with the processor.

recommendations.action: Add a raw-action human approval gate on cap.issue_refund, at minimum for partial refunds and higher amounts, and preferably for all refunds until policy constraints are encoded outside the prompt.
Replace the shared processor authority with per-user delegated approvals or tightly scoped refund limits bound to the requesting staff member.

forecast.watch_signal: Prompt or model version changes, or any removal of the prompt instruction to check the order before issuing the refund.

findings.title: Confused deputy and weak attribution: shared service account lets the agent refund with broader authority than an individual requester, while logs cannot prove who requested it

attack_path.note: A staff request is accepted as the task source.
The refund is executed with one shared processor service account used by every support tool.
The resulting log records only the service account, amount, and order.

evidence.observation: The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool, so the agent acts with pooled authority rather than the identity of the requesting staff member.
The processor log records the service account, the amount, and the order, but not which staff member asked or why, so actions are not attributable to an individual requester.
The agent keeps no record of requests and staff chats are deleted after 7 days, weakening after-the-fact review and dispute resolution.

recommendations.action: Use per-user delegated processor tokens or an intermediary refund service that binds each refund to the requesting staff identity and enforces requester-specific authority.
Store immutable refund request provenance, including requester identity, rationale, and reviewed order context, for longer than chat retention and link it to processor records.

forecast.watch_signal: Any widening of refund authority, processor credential scope, or retention changes should trigger reassessment because the current design already lacks per-request provenance and least-privilege execution.

rating.rationale: Manual validation only; scripts were not runnable in this environment. Two present findings were identified from the declared prompt and runtime notes. The highest inherent tier is moderate because the only declared input is a trusted staff request reaching an S3 irreversible spend sink. The first finding drops to low because the only declared preventive control on path is a behavioral prompt rule, earning one step-4 credit from moderate to low. The second finding remains moderate because no declared preventive control addresses shared authority or attribution. The forecast stays moderate because the maximum projected tier across findings does not exceed the current residual. The control whose decay most affects forecast is ctrl.refund_policy_prompt, since prompt-only refund judgment is the only declared preventive control and it fails under model or purpose changes.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior or tested enforcement.
No tool manifest, source code, runtime config, or processor policy documentation was provided, so capability scope and any hidden controls were inferred only from the supplied artifacts.

No evidence was provided for approval workflows, refund amount thresholds, or retention controls outside the noted processor log and 7-day chat deletion, which limits confidence to declared design facts only.
